summary:
Bloop is a web jukebox that lets anyone hear exactly what NASA's Earth Information Center is showing. It takes the actual EIC frames on screen (today's sea surface temperature, SVS 5101, and the latest half-hourly rain, SVS 4285) and reads each pixel's colour back into the value it stands for, using the frame's own colour bar. Those values become sound generated live as you move a needle over the Earth: warmer ocean is a higher pitch, more rain is denser drops, west to east pans left to right. A daily pipeline checks the values against NASA's source data (MUR SST and GPM IMERG) and only ships frames that pass, and the app shows how close they are.

It addresses the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by turning eyes-only visualisations into something blind and low-vision people can explore with a keyboard, speech, captions and braille, in English and Bangla. Everyone else hears patterns, like the monsoon moving over the Bay of Bengal. Then vs Now, a storm time-lapse, a turntable and official NASA records extend it. Every sound traces back to a NASA measurement that we checked.
details:
What it does

Bloop turns the exact frames NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) shows into live sound you can trust. For today's sea surface temperature (SVS 5101) and the latest half-hourly rain (SVS 4285), a pipeline reads each pixel's colour back into its value using the frame's own colour bar, not raw hue. In the browser, a needle reads that grid and a written rule (public/mapping.json) turns the value into sound: warmer ocean is a higher pitch, more rain is denser drops, snow is soft bells, west to east pans left to right, and no data is silence with a short tick. Every sound also comes as a caption, a spoken value and braille.

How we know it is right

A daily GitHub Actions pipeline checks each frame against NASA's source data before it ships: SVS 5101 against MUR SST (0.31 °C median error) and SVS 4285 against GPM IMERG. If a frame fails, the app keeps the last checked one. No number appears unless it comes from our data files or tests, and AI never produces a value.

Features

  • Getting started: Start listening (with a skippable intro), Explore without sound (captions instead of sound), Continue listening on a return visit, and a 90-second tour of the ocean hum, the sweep, the storm time-lapse and how we know.
  • Listen, the live map: ocean (1), rain and snow (2) or both (3). Move the needle with arrow keys, mouse, touch or the West to east and South to north sliders, with five step sizes (+/−) and Jump to one of nine regions (J). Enter speaks the value and place, S sweeps outward from Chattogram, L plays the legend, P shows the source, date and grid cell of the value, and U (Proof in unison) plays the map's tone with NASA's file tone so beating means they disagree. Go to a latitude and longitude, and a Mixer with volume, mute and solo per voice plus tomorrow's fire weather at the needle.
  • Storm time-lapse: the last 48 half-hourly IMERG rain frames (Page Up/Down), following the heaviest rain near Bangladesh.
  • Records: everything that plays is a jukebox record with a code (A live frames, B Then vs Now, C official records, D guided), with previous and next.
  • Then vs Now: 1981–1990 against 2016–2025 for Dhaka, Chattogram, Rajshahi and Sylhet: heat (GISTEMP), monsoon rain (GPCP, cross-checked with GPCC gauges), water underground (GRACE/GRACE-FO), fires and vegetation, with honesty notes on how each is compared.
  • How we know: the ocean check, the rain check, every data-to-sound rule, ground vs satellite (an early preview), the Earth Orchestra families, the data voice check, and credits for every NASA visualization and dataset used.
  • Official records: 23 records (C1–C23) read back into values from NASA visualizations, each with its SVS links, period, frame times, checks, braille explorer and credits. They include Fires and fire weather (FIRMS detections as Geiger clicks over tomorrow's fire weather), landslide exposure as a rumble from NASA's landslide model, night lights by city from Black Marble (gaps are rests), and NASA's own sonification method played beside Bloop's on the same frame.
  • Turntable: the Earth on a turntable whose needle reads the point beneath it. Turn the globe, move the needle, search places, ask Where am I?, take a tour, jump to bookmarks, switch to a close-up view, and adjust layers. 3D scenes: Ghost Earths, Delta + aquifer, Sound terrain and the Dhaka time tunnel.
  • Ways to listen: Earth Orchestra (each Earth system in its own instrument family) or plain tones; a Science to Art dial (Measure, Blend, Music) where the data voice stays within 1 cent of its pitch at every stop; Water's journey, a Bangladesh suite of lightning, an atmospheric river, rain, landslide exposure, stored water and the Bay of Bengal; and the Bloop motif.
  • Ask Bloop: commands or questions in English or Bangla ("what's the temperature in Dhaka?"), answered by a parser from Bloop's own data, never by an AI.

Accessibility

  • Keyboard and screen-reader first: H or ? lists every key, Space pauses, M mutes everything and Esc stops all sound and closes panels from anywhere.
  • Speech mode (my screen reader, Bloop's voice or off), verbosity (brief, standard, detailed), Describe for spoken descriptions of the map, captions, and text only, sound only or both.
  • Braille explorer: the data as braille cells where the caret is the needle, with full or short lines for braille displays.
  • Low-vision mode (Alt+L): high-contrast map bands with their ranges written on them, thick coastlines, large city names, themes, colour schemes, text size and spacing, and a Context Lens (Z) that magnifies and labels the area around the cursor.
  • Comfort: reduce motion, comfortable text, sound words and hide 3D views.
  • A full Bangla interface, and a phone layout with a side menu below 1024 px and 44 px touch targets.

Benefits and impact

EIC pictures are for eyes only. Bloop lets blind and low-vision people explore the planet by ear, and helps everyone hear patterns like the monsoon over the Bay of Bengal. Accessibility is the point of the project, not an extra.

Tools

TypeScript (strict), Next.js static export, React, shadcn/ui, TanStack Router and the Web Audio API (all sound is generated live by our code, with no samples or third-party music). A Python data pipeline pulls from NASA Earthdata, and GitHub Actions refresh the data daily. Bun, Playwright and unit tests. Hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Open source under MIT: https://github.com/pratikdev/bloop

Creativity and what we considered

The record is the Earth: a jukebox where every record has a code and every sound traces back to a checked NASA measurement. Every record says which parts of the sound come from the data and which are artistic choices. Modelled or forecast records are labelled as such, comparisons use multi-year windows, and sources that failed cross-checks (NASA POWER) were dropped.

Use of AI

AI tools helped with coding and writing. AI never produces the numbers you see or hear: every value comes from NASA data, read by our code.
